query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A DFT-based approach enhanced with on‐the‐fly machine learning can separately predict the lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than current thermodynamic models that conflate the two, yielding a prediction for lower lattice thermal conductivity (by roughly 15–20% at low temperatures) and overall conduction (within 10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures) with reduced prediction error (around 30% improvement).
generation.material_initial_state: Defect‐free, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy, with separate cases including high‐purity specimens and samples with 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Apply a predictive framework that integrates DFT-derived elastic properties with on-the-fly machine learning corrections, explicitly modeling lattice dynamics independently of electronic transport processes.
generation.conditions: Temperature range below 200 K (where lattice conduction dominates) and from 300 to 1200 K (where overall conductivity is relevant), comparing predictions for both pure and oxygen-doped specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale structure details that govern phonon scattering (including anharmonicity and oxygen-induced defect scattering) and electron-phonon interactions.
generation.mechanism: The model separately treats phonon-mediated (lattice) and electron-mediated heat transport. It captures the anharmonic lattice vibrations with machine learning corrections on DFT-based elastic properties, while using separate electronic structure methods for evaluating electronic contributions, thereby avoiding conflation of the two transport channels.
generation.predicted_outcome: At temperatures below 200 K, the approach will predict a lattice thermal conductivity about 15–20% lower than earlier conflated models, and at high temperatures (300–1200 K) the combined prediction for total thermal conductivity in oxygen-doped specimens will fall within the experimental range of 10–17 W/(K m) with an overall prediction error reduced by roughly 30%.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and DFT-based models that conflate lattice and electronic contributions, leading to less accurate predictions especially when separate transport regimes dominate.
generation.boundary: The model is validated for high-purity, defect‐free HfNbTaTiZr and controlled oxygen-doped variants. It may lose accuracy if additional impurity phases or significant microstructural defects are present.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements are estimated based on analogous developments in HEAs (as seen in studies of PbSnTeSe), the exact percentages of error reduction and the degree of separation between lattice and electronic contributions depend on detailed experimental calibration. Uncertainty remains high until targeted experiments confirm these metrics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity HfNbTaTiZr specimens and variants with 1 wt.% oxygen. Use temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements—employing techniques such as time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) for lattice conductivity and Hall-effect measurements for electronic conductivity—in two regimes: below 200 K (focusing on lattice contribution) and 300–1200 K (overall conductivity). Compare experimental data with the model’s separate predictions for lattice and electronic parts.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity for T < 200 K
Total thermal conductivity for 300 ≤ T ≤ 1200 K
Phonon dispersion curves (for lattice dynamics analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If experimental values for either the separated lattice or electronic thermal conductivities deviate by more than ±20% from the model predictions across the relevant temperature regimes—or if the predicted separation between lattice and electronic contributions cannot be observed experimentally—then the hypothesis that the new approach outperforms conflated models is falsified.

Investigation of PbSnTeSe High-Entropy Thermoelectric Alloy: A DFT Approach

Abstract: Thermoelectric materials have attracted extensive attention because they can directly convert waste heat into electric energy. As a brand-new method of alloying, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in the fields of materials science and engineering. Recent researches have found that HEAs could be potentially good thermoelectric (TE) materials. In this study, special quasi-random structures (SQS) of PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloys consisting of 64 atoms have been generated. The thermoelectric transport properties of the highest-entropy PbSnTeSe-optimized structure were investigated by combining calculations from first-principles density-functional theory and on-the-fly machine learning with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory and Green–Kubo theory. The results demonstrate that PbSnTeSe HEA has a very low lattice thermal conductivity. The electrical conductivity, thermal electronic conductivity and Seebeck coefficient have been evaluated for both n-type and p-type doping.
